title: The Head, The Eye, The Claw - Lore - Fable
text: General : The Head, The Eye, The Claw The City General Elysium Timeline Districts The Head is the leader of the Wings and the central governing body of the City. It is supported in its work by the Eye and the Claw. Overview The Head, the Eye, and the Claw are the three entities in direct control of A Corp., B Corp., and C Corp.—the Districts at the very center of the City—respectively. The Head governs over the other Wings and retains control over the entire City, being flanked in its functions by the Eye and the Claw. The Head does not typically interfere directly with the affairs of the various Wings in their own Districts; rather, its greatest involvement in the life of the City consists in establishing and enforcing the rules that relate to its overall ethics. This manifests in the Head carrying the power to establish the Taboos of the City: these must be observed in every District, by citizens and Wings, as the Head does not allow those who break them to live. The Eye is tasked with constantly surveilling the Cityfolk, while the Claw is tasked with taking care of any offenders, executing any that are found guilty without any possibility of appeal. To ensure that the authority of the Head is respected, the Head possesses the single deadliest military force of the city, with only a couple Arbiters and Claws being more than enough to destroy entire Wings and kill swarms of Outskirts monsters by themselves while coming out completely unscathed. Despite the Head's thorough control over the Nests, the Backstreets of the City can prove themselves to be difficult for the Head to manage due to direct opposition from the Five Fingers. While Taboos, notably ones related to Night in the Backstreets, still cannot be broken without punishment in these areas, the Fingers' efforts to keep the Backstreets in their control are notable enough that the Head cannot easily interfere with their businesses. Ethics The Head's will shapes the image of the City, as it wields the ability to decide when a part of it no longer fits in the vision, and to chase it outside its confines. Some speculate the Head's decisions in these matters aren't aimed at maintaining order, but rather that the Head wishes to preserve its ideal image of the City, and that for this reason they allow the various Stars of the City to keep existing, being aware of their importance to the Cityfolk. This is corroborated by the agents of the Head themselves referring to their work as cultivating the "ecology" of the City. To preserve this vision, the Head retains the unique power to assign the highest risk level in the scale of hazards of the City, that of Impuritas Civitatis, or Impurity of the City. The risk level of Impurity signifies a hazard that violates the ethics of the City, and that must be either destroyed or physically expelled from the confines of the City expeditiously. As part of this action, the Head introduced the Artificial Intelligence Ethics Amendment, which established City-wide Taboos against creating artificial beings with autonomy comparable to that of humans, regardless of their appearance, material, or method of creation. As with other Taboos of the City, ending the violation is typically more important than capturing the violator; if an unauthorized artificial being is deprived of that autonomous capacity, the Head no longer considers its continued existence to be a breach of this Taboo. Notably, the Taboo does not include non-sapient monsters, such as the Whales of the Great Lake or the Trash Crabs of U Corp.'s District, and monstrous creatures of human origin, such as Distortions,Abnormalities, or Bloodfiends. Whether a being's existence effectively breaks a Taboo is ultimately up to the Head, as can be seen by the Head being responsible for patenting the liquid and method that allows the creation of Sweepers. Furthermore, the Head released a treaty that established a Taboo against the resurrection of a human being, although forms of revival done through time manipulation seem to be permitted. The Head has also set a number of restrictions on the creation and distribution of firearms, including limits on the Workshops that produce them, and on human cloning, which allow two copies of the same person to exist in the City for no longer than seven days according to A Corp.'s time scale. The Head is responsible for various other Taboos of the City, which are effective in all Districts, such as not paying one's taxes, violating a residential area during the Night in the Backstreets, surveillance and recordings during the Night in the Backstreets—including attempts at investigating any incidents that occurred during the event— and unauthorized usage of patented technologies. The punishment for violating the Taboos established by the Head is noted to be different from breaking a Taboo of a Nest, which usually involves being chased by a small number of Taboo hunters. Breaking a Taboo of the City is believed to be equivalent to a death sentence, and for a Wing, it results in the stripping of its qualifications and immediate shutdown. The Head The Head's identity is completely unknown, although it appears the term refers to a group of people rather than a singular entity. Any detail regarding said identity is a closely guarded secret. Through A Corp., the Head is responsible for authorizing Wings, managing patents and payment of fines related to them, and for the minting of dollars, the currency used in the City. Through the Eye, the Head also watches over the citizens of the City constantly, with particular attention to the work of Wings and other Corporations. The Head is in control of the Sweepers. Sweepers are expected to abide to a set of rules provided by the Head, and they respond to it directly. The Head has been shown to make use of the Sweepers to clean the remains of a site following its destruction at the hands of Arbiters and Claws, as punishment for the breaking of a major Taboo. Arbiters Arbiters are the agents of the Head. Augmented through various Singularities, Arbiters wield incredible power, capable of taking down entire Wings. Arbiters appear to be a specialized unit for dealing with Impurities of the City. It is suggested that only one Arbiter is typically deployed, at the head of a group of Claws. Arbiters are augmented through Singularities and are able to utilize them in combat, being often seen making use of F Corp.'s fairies. They also have an ability to quickly teleport out of situations should they deem it necessary. Arbiters typically have human appearances, and wear a uniform featuring long black robes with golden highlights and hexagonal patterns. Should an Arbiter find themselves stripped of their title, they will have any memory related to the secrets of the Head wiped, ensuring that even the smallest bit of information remains secure. The Head also retrieves the corpses of former or deceased Arbiters, likely to prevent other parties from extracting information from them. It can be assumed that this procedure may apply to Claws and Beholders as well, as they too are privy to the Head's secrets. The Eye and the Claw Beholders The role of the Eye is to monitor the people of the City, watchful for any threats to the authority of the Head. The Eye's gaze extends to the confines of the City, but typically not beyond them, unless in search of a specific threat. Its agents are called Beholders, but are rarely referred to as "Eyes". Unlike Claws and Arbiters, Beholders are not involved in physical combat. However, Beholders are sent out along with Arbiters and Claws as they destroy Impurity-level threats in the form of static glass panels or chambers, monitoring the situation from a distance. Claws The duty of the Claw is to bring punishment down upon those who break the Taboos of the Head, and swiftly remove any threat to the City. The Executioners are agents of the Claw, and are typically only referred to as "Claws". Executioners are augmented through different methods, sporting prosthetic heads and clawed arms, to which are attached Serums that supposedly make use of various Singularities. Claws are typically seen making use of these Serums to enhance their abilities during combat, such as: Serum K, which allows for regeneration, likely derived from K Corp.'s Singularity; Serum W, which appears to make use of W Corp.'s space-bending Singularity; Serum R, which may make use of R Corp.'s Singularity to enhance attacks. Beyond these, it appears they have a wider array of Serums at their disposal, as seen during the fall of the Kong Family, where one is seen using a purple-colored Serum ability. As the purple-colored Serum ability is visually represented as claw marks, this Serum might be connected to C Corp.'s own Singularity. Like Arbiters, they also have an ability to teleport to or from a given area when needed. Claws are tasked with dealing with the breaking of lesser City Taboos, such as eliminating clones that have survived past the seven day limit. They also accompany Arbiters during their visits to the sites of major Taboo violations.

title: Lore - Fable
text: Lore The City General Elysium Timeline Districts Overview The City of Elysium is an urban mega structure the size of a small country, it has a population of around 7 billion spread apart by 14 layers and 26 districts. The City sits above The Ruins which holds it up above The Wastes. Districts The City is divided into twenty-six Districts, quite diverse in culture and aesthetics, each of which is governed by a Wing, a corporation that has ascended to claim complete control of said area. All Wings respond to the Head, the supreme governing power of the City. The arrangement of the Districts seems to be static, as there has been no mentioned case of a District expanding into a fallen Wing's territory. Each District is split into a Nest, a territory directly governed and protected by its Wing, and the Backstreets, expansive spaces of wilderness or slums, largely neglected by the Wings, where the Syndicates of the City run free. The Head The Head is the leader of the Wings and the central governing body of the City. It is in direct control of A Corp., B Corp., and C Corp., the three Districts at the peak of the City. The Head's identity is completely unknown, although it appears the term refers to a group of people rather than a singular entity; any detail regarding it is a closely guarded secret. The Head, through A Corp., retains control of the entire City. It is responsible for authorizing Wings, managing patents, and the minting of dollars, the currency used in the City. Despite this, it does not typically interfere directly with the affairs of the various Wings in their own Districts; rather, the Head's greatest involvement in the life of the City consists in establishing and enforcing the rules that relate to the overall ethics of the City. The Head's will shapes the image of the City, as it wields the ability to decide when a part of it no longer fits in the vision, and to chase it outside its confines. Some speculate the Head's decisions in these matters aren't aimed at maintaining order, but rather that the Head wishes to preserve its ideal image of the City, and that for this reason they allow the various Stars of the City to keep existing. This is corroborated by the agents of the Head themselves referring to their work as cultivating the ecology of the City. To preserve this vision, the Head retains the unique power to assign the highest risk level in the scale of hazards of the City, that of Impuritas Civitatis, or Impurity of the City. The risk level of Impurity signifies a hazard that violates the ethics of the City, and that must be either destroyed or physically expelled from the confines of the City expeditiously. The Head introduced the Artificial Creature Ethics Amendment, which established a City-wide Taboo against creating artificial beings with autonomy comparable to that of humans, regardless of their form, material, or method of creation. The Taboo concerns autonomy rather than whether a being resembles a human. The Head has also set a number of restrictions on the creation and distribution of advanced firearms and on human cloning, which allow two copies of the same person to exist in the City for no longer than seven days. It is also a City-wide Taboo to record a spell on digital media. A spell may be preserved only in a written book, such as a spellbook, or retained in the caster’s memory; no recording, file, device, or other digital storage can lawfully contain its formula. This prohibition applies whether the spell is copied, transmitted, photographed, scanned, or stored as data. The Head is also responsible for various other Taboos of the City, such as not paying one's taxes, and violating a residential area during the Night in the Backstreets. The punishment for breaking any of these Taboos usually involve physical extermination, and for a Wing, the stripping of its qualifications and immediate shutdown. The punishment for violating the Taboos established by the Head is noted to be different from breaking a Taboo of a Nest, which usually involves being chased by a small number of Taboo hunters; breaking a Taboo of the City is believed to be equivalent to a death sentence. The Head is backed up in its functions by the Eye and the Claw, the two authorities responsible for B Corp. and C Corp. respectively. In enforcing the laws of the City, the three Wings make use of three types of agents: the Arbiters, the Beholders, and the Claws. When handling an Impurity-level threat, these agents are qualified to expel an entity from the City itself and move it into The Wastes. Wings and Nests The Wings of the World are a group of the twenty-six largest, most powerful conglomerates in the City. Each Wing acts as the governing body of a Nest of the City's District, and is commonly referred to with a letter from A to Z, corresponding to the number of the District in their control. Wings generally oversee all facets of living in the Nest of their District, while leaving the residents of the Backstreets to fend for themselves. A Nest is the urban center of a District, which is under the direct management of its Wing. The citizens and employees of a Wing are commonly referred to as "feathers"; the status of a feather is widely considered one of the best and most secure paths in life, which the people of the Backstreets are often willing to go to great lengths to obtain. To gain access to a Nest, a corresponding Nest migration permit is required, while to be granted temporary passage one must be in possession of a visa unique to the specific Nest. Visas are implied to be relatively common, with corporate employees being provided with work visas that allow them as easy passage; Nest migration permits, on the other hand, are highly sought after, and implied to be expensive enough that even Grade 1 Fixers would struggle to obtain them. During the Smoke War, migration permits were offered as rewards to Fixers participating for K Corp. and I Corp., although by the end of the war the veterans were refused entry to the Nests. Each Wing has its own cultural style and social structure which are reflected in how it governs its Nest, and the policies that regulate the way of life in the District's Backstreets. The laws of a Wing are called Taboos, and are enforced by specialized Fixers called Taboo hunters that police both the Nest and the Backstreets. While all Wings have Taboos, the enforcement and punishment for breaking them varies. The Wings are directly ruled over by the Head, which bestows the status on a corporation that possesses and is able to successfully utilize a Singularity, a unique form of technology that is able to break the laws of physics. As such, the Wings closely guard any information about their Singularity, employing military forces from their own ranks or from those of their business partners to avoid losing its secrets to rival Wings, industry competitors, or other forces. If a Wing's technology is stolen, fails commercially, or is viewed unfavorably by the Head, a Wing can collapse, resulting in the Nest losing its protection and being encroached by various factions that vie for its control, such as the Syndicates of the Backstreets. After a Wing collapses, a different corporation can attempt to ascend to the status of a Wing for that District. Backstreets The Backstreets are the areas of a District that lay outside the Wing's domain. The Backstreets are typically slums crowded with buildings, characterized by twisted and irregular roads, although there can be great differences between Districts. Wings have differing degrees of presence, influence, and benevolence with regards to their Backstreets, although their relationship is ultimately exploitative. Citizens of the Backstreets are motivated to move up the ladder and into the Nests, while citizens of the Nests are motivated to maintain their statuses and preserve a more comfortable life under their Wing's protection. While not as secure as the Nest, residential areas are the safest parts of the Backstreets. Given how strongly Backstreets denizens wish for a life in the Nest, Wings tend to uphold strict divides between the sectors, including security checkpoints and physical divisions. Security of borders between Nests and Backstreets vary from plasma walls to mere chain fences, but the Wings' power is such that no one in the Backstreets dares to cross over into a Nest without express permission. As the Backstreets are not under the control and protection of the Wings, and even the Head's power struggles to reach within them, various factions operate freely in their place. The Backstreets are home to the headquarters of both Fixers, a type of mercenary for hire, who typically operate their Offices in the Backstreets, and organizations and gangs called Syndicates. Among Syndicates, the most important are the Five Fingers, the five largest Syndicates of the City which most other Syndicates answer to, and whose power is said to rival that of the Wings. The Night in the Backstreets is another defining component of Backstreets life, as an 80 minute phenomena taking place from 3:14 to 4:34 AM. During this time period, nearly everything is allowed, as no one is held responsible for their deeds done during this time period. It is considered a brazenly savage, brutal, and vulgar period, even for the City. Beings known as Sweepers routinely become active during the Night in the Backstreets, and sweep through the streets in waves in order to consume any objects and structures located outside of permitted residential buildings, erasing all evidence of crime. The Night in the Backstreets are regulated by only two Taboos: that residential areas mustn't be destroyed or violated in any way, including forcing the doors open, and that nothing which occurs during the Night in the Backstreets is recorded. The only form of testimony allowed during the Night in the Backstreets are direct eyewitnesses; even then, it is a Taboo mandated by the Head that no activity during this period are to be reported on. While the rules of the Night in the Backstreet don't apply to the Nest, it's viable to drag a Nest citizen into the Backstreets and dispose of them in this manner. Culture Magic is another part of the City’s shared vocabulary. A spell is a deliberate, limited shaping of the raw magic that suffuses the world, and its use is taught, inherited, researched, bought, or carried through Relics. Cantrips are practiced often enough to be cast at will, while more demanding spells require preparation or a spell fixed in the caster’s mind. A spellbook, a focus, a component pouch, and the correct material components can be as ordinary to a trained worker as a set of tools, though never equally affordable in every District. The details of casting matter in public life. Verbal components make some magic impossible to hide; somatic components require a free hand; expensive material components can turn a useful spell into a luxury. Rituals offer a slower, less costly alternative when time permits. A tenant may use Alarm to protect a room, a researcher may use Identify to study an object, and a courier may depend on Sending when ordinary communication is unreliable. The City’s people use the languages listed in the Standard and Exotic Languages rules, alongside regional languages and dialects. Some languages are families with many dialects, while others survive only in old records. Sweepers also speak a secret language of their own. Various levels of education exist in the City. Schools exist both in the Nests and in the Backstreets, although other options are available, such as boarding schools and virtual schooling, both of which are considered safer options, as it allows the students to not have to cross dangerous alleyways on their way to school. In the Nest, homeschooling is shown to be an option as well. The currency of the City is called dollars. It appears to be a common currency across the City, though with some exceptions, such as District 20, in which citizens commonly use their time, regulated through T Corp.'s Singularity, as currency. Money is extremely important to the people of the City, to the point it is a common belief that it can be used to solve any problem. The City is also characterized by great income gaps, both between the people of the Backstreets and the Nest, and among the people of the Nest itself, where only the higher classes can live comfortably, while the majority of the citizens use most of their income in living expenses and taxes, and don't have the ability to save up for emergencies. Clothing styles show great variation between the four quarters of the City. The fashion of the south is mostly inspired by real-life 21st century, western formal aesthetics, though with exceptions such as T Corp., where the fashion is instead inspired by the 19th century steampunk aesthetic the District is based on. The fashion of the east is instead based on real-life eastern, particularly Chinese fashion, ranging from traditional clothing to more modern interpretations. The clothing of the east, like that of the north and south, is mentioned to be mostly cloth-based. Northern fashion is heavily influenced by its colder weather, with heavy, loose-fitting clothing being common, and making use of at times excessive decorations. The fashion of the west makes use of leather over cloth, and is noted to often include metal armor in its trends. Western fashion appears to be inspired by the real-life Middle Ages in Europe, borrowing elements from medieval armor. City People Spellcasting does not erase the City’s inequality. A cantrip may be available to someone who has practiced it, but a higher-level spell consumes spell points and a caster can only recover that resource through rest. Healing magic, protective wards, divinations, and mobility spells can change the outcome of a bad day, yet the training, time, components, and safe place to rest remain easier to secure in a Nest than in the Backstreets. A Relic that grants a spell can be a lifeline, an inheritance, or a debt that binds its bearer to an employer or Syndicate. Everyday life in the City is defined by a constant struggle to stay afloat. While the people of The Wastes dream of living in the City, which they see as a safe place from the monsters that plague it, the people of the Backstreets strive to gain the wealth and power to gain access to a Nest, partially due to the influence of the Wings publicizing Nest dwellers' lives as the height of prosperity and comfort, and the people of the Nest struggle daily to keep their place inside it, while being constantly exploited by the Wings. Regardless of their station, the people of the City are never free, and in order to survive, they typically tie themselves to various forms of organizations, seeking security and belonging in something larger than them. In doing so, they're willing to exploit others beneath them and make use of all the City can offer them, without caring about anyone else's well-being, and often taking pleasure in their suffering. The people of the Backstreets must typically tie themselves to one of the Five Fingers or their subsidiaries to receive the necessary protection to carry on with their lives, while the people of the Nests depend on the Wings to shelter them. Because of this, Nest dwellers are colloquially known as "feathers". While the high level of security the Nest provides makes it the most ideal place to reside, its daily routine, which is often accompanied by overtime work and the constant fear of losing one's job and place in the Nest, can be stifling and oppressive to many of its citizens, with some recalling becoming listless as if they "lost focus, spacing out and staring into empty places". The necessity for a connection to a group also means that the people of the City try not to form strong connections between individuals, as personal bonds can become a hindrance in one's abilities in the case of a loved one's death, which proves to be especially dangerous for those involved in Fixer work. The Cityfolk are still generally accustomed to such events, and it is not considered uncommon for them to swiftly move on by searching for a substitute. In general, death, including mass casualties, is a common occurrence in the City. People all over the City are greatly accustomed to this, to the point even cases of 80,000 casualties are considered, while distressing, not particularly shocking, and not important enough to require special attention unless they happen to be within a Nest. Due to the frequency of such events, Cityfolk must learn to hide their grief and deal with it quickly, reflecting on the practice of funerals being uncommon in the City. Backstreets dweller instead typically let the bodies of the deceased be taken away during the Night in the Backstreets, to avoid the grave be desecrated by robbers looking to steal valuables of prosthetics from the body. Furthermore, the availability of technologies such as prosthetic substitution, the ability to quickly reconstruct flesh, and Life Insurance in many ways trivialize pain and death itself for those who can afford it, leaving their users insensitive to such dangers. These factors have led to the people of the City becoming apathetic and uncaring of other people's suffering, living without allowing themselves to truly feel their emotions and wishes, and lacking the curiosity to learn about the world they inhabit and the technologies they make use of every day, instead preferring to shut out reality altogether whenever possible. The L Corp. researcher Alice would come to describe these traits as a "disease of the mind", that plagued the people of the City, and that if left alone, it would bring them all to destruction. Lobotomy Corporation's work began as an attempt to cure this disease, and the Distortion phenomenon would be born in its aftermath. The Cityfolk's feelings manifest in different ways as well. Their desires are mentioned to beget concepts comparable to "gods", such as the Prescripts of the Index, which are generated from the people's wish for a direction in life. This same desire is what often brings the Cityfolk to join cults that promise to grant them a purpose, such as the Church of Gears. Beyond these forms, however, the City currently lacks major forms of organized religion, although it is suggested that they have existed in the past. Fixers & Association In the City, a common path in life for those without better options is that of the Fixer. A Fixer is a sort of handyman, who can be hired for everything from menial tasks to active combat. Fixers are subject to a grading system based on the missions they complete. A Fixer starts at Grade 9 and can be promoted to a higher grade, all the way up to 1; in the case of a Fixer being caught breaking work regulations, they can lose their status and be demoted to a lower grade. A majority of Fixers congregate in Fixer Offices, small to mid-sized businesses led by and composed of Fixers. Offices process requests dedicated to whomever in their ranks may be best suited. Offices can work independently, or they can be associated with particular Associations of Fixers, which are larger professional organizations with City-wide influence, with particular interests aimed at the Fixers working beneath them. There are twelve Associations in the City, each of which manages certain types of requests common to Fixer work, such as the Zwei Association focusing on protection missions, or the Devyat' Association focusing on delivery across the City. Associations control and distribute Fixer tasks, and can take jobs from anywhere within the City, as they have individual branches set up in various Districts. Branches are divided into four groups corresponding to the cardinal directions of the City, and employees are further divided by grade into sections ranging from 1 to 6, with lower number sections corresponding to higher Fixer grades. Every Association has its own rules, specialties, uniform, and agreements with other factions. The Associations are governed by the Hana Association, which oversees everything related to the Fixer system, including Fixer grades. In the case of a Grade 1 Fixer demonstrating great renown in any particular field of work, they may be considered beyond the grading system, and receive the title of Color from Hana Association as a way to signify their exceptional skill. Color Fixers can keep working in their Offices, or be contracted by a company. They are admired throughout the City, and it is a common belief that the life of a Color is one of true freedom. Despite this, Color Fixers are still bound to the regulations of Hana Associations and of the Head, and due to their ability they're often made to handle the most dangerous hazards of the City. Fixer work gives spellcasting a practical place alongside weapons, augments, and contracts. An Office may take a protection request that calls for Alarm , Mage Armor , or Protection from Evil and Good ; an investigation may require Detect Magic , Identify , or Zone of Truth ; and a pursuit can turn on Misty Step , Darkness , or Dispel Magic . These are tools rather than guarantees. A caster still needs the range, components, time, and concentration stated by the spell, and a Fixer in armor must be proficient with it to cast at all. Syndicates Syndicates are a type of organization in the City, and can be seen as the unregulated counterpart to Fixer Offices, being comparable to gangs with various goals and methods of operating. In general, the term Syndicate is used to refer to organized groups that aren't tied to the responsibilities and restrictions that come with being a Fixer. Some Syndicates focus on extorting money from people for protection, while others abduct people, kill for fun and pleasure, or do anything in between. Syndicates mostly operate in the Backstreets, but are not restricted to them. They can be small groups that only exist in one corner of the Backstreets, or large enough to exist in every District in the City. Syndicates can be hired to do contract jobs, although there is higher risk compared to contracting an Office or Association, as they are not bound to the same regulations Fixers are. Sometimes, Wings will hire Syndicate members for criminal projects that cannot be handled officially. Syndicates tend to have a culture unique to their group, and a way of living that distinguishes them from other Syndicates. Many Syndicates have a culture focused around replicating family dynamics and consider each other family, with some even referring to each other with familial terms. This can result in Syndicates with a strict focus on respect for those who are higher ranked, or in Syndicates whose members care deeply for each other and protect one another at any cost. Syndicates are graded through the City's hazard system, measuring their danger level and notability. Syndicates can grow under these aspects and gain power in many ways, with one of them being the practice of raiding and wiping out Fixers' Offices. The larger and more experienced an Office is, the greater the notoriety that is achieved by defeating it. Above all Syndicates are the Five Fingers, or "the hand of the Backstreets", five Star of the City-level Syndicates, whose power rivals that of the Wings. Each of the Five Fingers has a distinct culture, and demands different things from people seeking protection under them. Other Syndicates can become subsidiaries of the Five Fingers, granting them powerful connections as long as they abide by the Finger's orders. Technology Denizens of the City have developed a wide variety of fantastical technologies that they use on a daily basis. People from all quarters of the City make ample use of body modification procedures, which allow individuals to augment their strength or replace lost body parts. Prosthetic substitution involves the replacement of organic parts with mechanical or bionic ones, making it possible for a person to replace their entire body, with the exception of the brain. Due to the Head's Taboo against copies of human bodies, this makes the sight of an individual with mechanical limbs or a display in place of their head incredibly common in the City. Furthermore, City denizens can make use of various types of life insurance policy, such as the one provided by H Corp., that allow resuscitation after death. Thanks to these policies, individuals who can afford the cost can be brought back to life in a new body without violating the Head's Ethics Amendment, as long as their brain remained intact. Augmentation procedures are also used by a large demographic of people, from Syndicate members to wealthy Nest citizens. Augmentation is particularly common among those involved in Fixer business, to the point it's considered virtually impossible to do Fixer work without investing in augmentation procedures. Through these procedures, an individual might obtain superhuman speed or strength, or strengthen their body parts to become impervious to various types of attacks. The technological innovation of the City also reflects on its healthcare. Through the research of the Wings and the power of their Singularities, such of K Corp.'s and H Corp.'s, nearly every health problem has become curable on a theoretical level. In practice, only those who can afford it are able to pay to make use of these technologies. This goes for most of the innovation of the City. In most cases, these technologies are available at various levels of quality, with the most expensive and safe being used by Nest citizens, while the people of the Backstreets can make use of cheaper versions that can cause unwanted side effects, as is the case for memory wipe procedures. Magic and technology are intertwined without being the same thing. A spell produces a discrete effect when a caster shapes magic; a device, prosthetic, or Singularity is a constructed system that may sustain an effect, package it as a service, or exploit a principle no ordinary spell can reproduce. A clinic might use surgery, an H Corp. policy, and spells such as Cure Wounds or Lesser Restoration in the same treatment, while still reserving its safest care for those who can pay. Despite the level of innovation of the City generally being incredibly high, its access isn't uniform across the various Districts. While cell phones, the Internet, and various public transport systems exist, they are not universally available. For example, advanced communication systems aren't available in T Corp.'s District, with its citizens making use of letters instead. Singularities A Singularity should not be confused with a spell, even when both create an effect that looks miraculous. A spell is a bounded expression of magic with a casting time, range, components, duration, and a caster’s limits. A Singularity is a proprietary source of industrial power whose effects can reorganize a District’s transport, medicine, labor, warfare, or environment. The distinction is why a Wing protects a Singularity as a state secret while ordinary spellcasting remains part of the City’s daily life. Singularities are the technologies that define the Wings. They are not merely advanced inventions: each is an impossible principle, object, process, or system that can violate the ordinary limits of the world. A corporation that can possess, exploit, and protect a Singularity gains the military strength and revenue required to seek Wing status; a Wing that loses control of its Singularity risks collapse. The modern order of Wings began when a traveler from The Ruins brought Z Corp. an object infused with the power of The Wastes. Its discovery changed the corporate arms race. Weapons and spells alone had become too costly to distinguish one corporation from another, but a Singularity could create an entire industry, make a District indispensable, and give its owner a form of power no competitor could reproduce reliably. No two Singularities need resemble one another. Their known effects range from restoration and preservation to the manipulation of gravity, time, dreams, containment, locking, erasure, virtual experience, and space. They may appear as a manufactured device, a natural or recovered object, a procedure, an environment, or a service. The product sold to the public is often only a controlled application of the underlying phenomenon. District life is shaped by the Singularity of its Wing. G Corp. uses gravity manipulation for artificial wings, levitating vehicles, and its floating Nest. T Corp. turns time and light into resources. W Corp.’s Singularity harnesses Warp, the radiation-like energy that emanates from The Ruins and The Wastes, to promise travel between distant parts of the City in seconds. K Corp. and H Corp. turn their medical technologies into healing, agriculture, bodily alteration, and weapons. Each benefit has a price, a patent, and an owner. A Singularity is also a secret worth killing for. Wings compartmentalize their research, employ corporate forces and contracted Fixers, erase records, and conduct wars to keep competitors from learning how it works. Imitations and stolen derivatives circulate through the City, but they are unreliable, dangerous, or illegal precisely because they lack the original owner’s control. A Singularity can be bought around, copied imperfectly, or fought over, but never treated as an ordinary commodity. The Ruins remain a source of both relics and unknown Singularities. Delvers, Fixer expeditions, corporate prospectors, and scavengers descend in search of them. Their discoveries can raise a corporation into a Wing, destabilize a District, or create a new hazard before anyone understands what was found. Hazards Magic changes how hazards are investigated and answered, not whether they are dangerous. A Fixer can search for a lingering magical effect, counter a spell with Dispel Magic , shelter a group behind an abjuration, or use divination to find a missing person. None of that guarantees safety against an abnormality, a Distortion, a hostile caster, or a failing Singularity. Area spells can also turn a crowded Backstreets fight into a larger disaster, which is why responsible Offices treat a caster’s range, target, and area of effect as part of the job’s risk. A hazard is any threat that endangers people, a District, a Wing’s interests, or the City’s imposed order. Hazards are not limited to monsters. A hostile Syndicate, a failed Singularity, a Distortion, a contaminated excavation site, a corporate military operation, an escaped abnormality, or a public disaster can all be treated as hazards depending on the damage they cause and the attention they attract. The City grades hazards by danger and notability. This makes the classification political as well as practical: an event that destroys Backstreets lives may be ignored, contained, or quietly exploited, while the same threat inside a Nest can bring immediate corporate action. Fixer Offices and Associations take paid requests against lower-scale threats; Wings deploy their own forces when the threat affects a District’s profits, image, or Singularity. Some dangers are recognized as Stars of the City. A Color Fixer, the Five Fingers, a powerful Syndicate, or another extraordinary force can reach that level of notoriety. A Star is not automatically an enemy. It is a force whose ability and influence are too great for the City to dismiss, and whose continued existence may be tolerated so long as it does not violate The Head’s vision. The highest designation is Impuritas Civitatis , an Impurity of the City. The Head assigns this classification only to something it considers fundamentally incompatible with the City’s ethics. A City-wide Taboo, an autonomous artificial creature, an unlawful human copy, or a threat that overturns the established order can be judged an Impurity. The purpose of the designation is not negotiation: the subject must be destroyed or expelled through The Ruins into The Wastes. Responses depend on the scale of the threat. Taboo hunters enforce a Wing’s local laws. Offices, Associations, and contracted Syndicates deal with work that can be paid for or denied publicly. The Eye, the Claw, Arbiters, Beholders, and Claws act when The Head intervenes. This hierarchy ensures that many hazards are handled as business before they are recognized as disasters. Monsters Monsters are part of Elysium’s environment, not an anomaly outside it. Some are creatures surviving in The Wastes amid godblood, Warp, and distorted mana. Others emerge from The Ruins, where dead gods, buried kingdoms, lost technologies, relics, and damaged reality lie beneath the City. Expeditions into those places are valuable because of what they can recover, but they are never safe. District Z demonstrates the City’s relationship with monsters most clearly. Its excavation and dredging work supplies Elysium with durable metals, relics, and possible Singularities. Old sites and collapsed tunnels are often left behind once they stop being profitable, becoming hellholes inhabited by Warp-touched life. The Wing does not make extermination its first priority; people who enter to scavenge are expected to accept the risk. Some creatures are the results of corporate use rather than wilderness. The Smoke War left insect-like prosthetic survivors and refugees in its wake. H Corp.’s biological products can alter bodies and create animal-like combatants. The Great Lake of District U contains enormous Whales and distinct biomes governed by their own conditions. A monster may be a natural survivor, a changed person, a manufactured weapon, or the unintended consequence of a Wing’s technology. Gift Gnomes and other peoples of the City should not be confused with monsters simply because they are unusual. The Head’s historic age of humanity and its Taboos concern status, autonomy, and control; corporate propaganda often blurs those distinctions when it serves a Wing’s interests. In practice, the City’s institutions decide what is called a creature, a citizen, a product, or a hazard. Monsters are also distinct from abnormalities and Distortions. Abnormalities began appearing after the White Nights and Dark Days from the devastation surrounding L Corp.’s branches. Distortions arise when a person’s emotion, desire, and despair overwhelm their human form. Both may be treated as monsters by witnesses and corporations, but their origins are tied to the City’s history and the unresolved legacy of L Corp., E.G.O, and Alice’s research. Sweepers Sweepers are creatures that become active during the Night in the Backstreets, the eighty minutes from 3:14 to 4:34 AM. They travel through the Backstreets in waves and consume what is left outside permitted residential buildings: bodies, possessions, structures, evidence, and the remains of violence. For residents, the warning to get indoors before the Night is not custom. It is survival. Their work gives the Night its particular cruelty. Nearly anything can happen during those eighty minutes, yet the Sweepers remove the physical evidence before the morning. This does not make the Night lawless. Two City-wide Taboos remain absolute: a residential area cannot be destroyed or violated, including by forcing open a door, and nothing that occurs during the Night may be recorded or reported. Only direct eyewitness testimony is permitted, and even that cannot become a report of the Night’s events. The prohibition protects the City’s silence as much as it regulates the creatures. A person may be dragged from a Nest into the Backstreets and disposed of during the Night, while the Nest itself remains outside the Night’s ordinary rules. Sweepers speak a secret language. It is separate from the Standard and Exotic Languages used by City people, from regional dialects, and from the terminology of the Associations. Knowledge that the language exists does not grant an ordinary speaker the ability to understand it; it remains a guarded and alien part of Backstreets life. Backstreets residents build their routines around the Night. Bodies are often left for the Sweepers rather than buried, both because death is common and because graves invite robbers seeking valuable prosthetics. The result is a City where disappearance, cleanup, and silence are treated as normal conditions of life. History The City’s history begins with the collapse of the Old World. Before gods and magic became part of mortal life, humanity possessed weapons and technology capable of reaching beyond its world. Contact with the gods of other worlds brought curiosity, greed, jealousy, and eventually war. Human nations divided around divine powers, and the old order gave way to an empire shaped by faith, arcana, and the occult. The Empire was not simply a human nation. It was a tool through which pantheons exercised influence over the world. Mortals who resisted were overwhelmed by powers their former defenses could not match. The brief peace after the Empire’s victory failed because the gods themselves lacked a common purpose. Their followers turned upon one another in the Empyrean War. The Empyrean War joined divine magic to the world-ending weapons that the Old World had refused to use. Gods and mortals built devices capable of poisoning reality itself. Cornered powers chose mutual destruction rather than submission. When the war ended, the world below was molten and scarred by Warp, dead gods, godblood, and distorted mana: the place now known as The Wastes. That war also explains why magic in Elysium is treated with both familiarity and caution. The same art can provide a ward, repair a wound, reveal a hidden truth, or destroy a street. The City’s spellcasters work within rules of preparation, components, range, and finite spell points, but the memory of magic combined with unrestricted technology remains embedded in corporate policy, military research, and The Head’s fear of anything it cannot contain. Surviving peoples were evacuated into demiplanes, but those shelters could only support them temporarily. As resources dwindled and faith weakened, the gods and mortals needed a permanent refuge. The Ruins, a protected catacomb for dead mortals, rulers, dragons, and gods, had survived the wars as a memorial. The decision to build on it was contested as desecration, but the alternative was to leave the living without a home. Laborers and craftsmen raised Elysium above The Ruins. Space demanded vertical construction, and the City grew into a layered megastructure rather than spreading across the poisoned world. Most gods were gone, dead, weakened, or left behind as the survivors of many peoples became concentrated within one structure. In AE 56, segregation and conflict allowed arms profiteers to turn fear into wealth and political power. Regulations and social classes were presented as protection, while separating the influential from the poor. In AE 74, this new ruling order named itself The Head. It divided the City into Districts, placed A, B, and C at the peak, and formalized the divide between Nests and Backstreets. The Head allowed major corporations to govern individual Districts because it could not manage every layer directly. Their rivalry became the War of the Wings. In AE 184, Z Corp. received an object from a traveler out of The Ruins: a Singularity. By AE 185, the ability to harness a Singularity became central to a corporation’s claim to Wing status. The Smoke War, the fall of L Corp., the White Nights and Dark Days, and the emergence of abnormalities, Distortions, and E.G.O all followed within the City’s later history. The Elysium Timeline tab preserves the chronological record in full, from the Old World to the present City. The Districts tab records how that history remains visible in each Wing’s culture, technology, Nest, and Backstreets. Nests were the common living places for the middle and upper classes, while Backstreets were the slums where the poor and outcasts were left to survive. The Head placed itself at the top of the city in District A, with Districts B and C underneath it, and so on. The price of living in each District was naturally based on its verticality: the higher Districts were farther from The Ruins and Warp in The Wastes, while District Z stood one fall away from The Ruins and endured daily Warp exposure. Then came the corporations. The city had large numbers of corporations, but The Head couldn't manage each District at the same time, so it allowed large enough corporations to gain the ability to create and enforce laws within the specific Districts they governed. This created conflict that would become known as the War of the Wings. AE 184 The Wings The Wings are large corporations able to create and enforce laws within the Districts they govern. A Wing can be overthrown if its revenue and shares no longer meet the threshold needed to sustain its District, or if its owner and board members are killed by rival corporations. As conflicts progressed, each corporation that became a Wing found it difficult to maintain its status through an arms race of weapons and spells that no one could keep up with. This changed when a traveler from The Ruins came to Z Corp., the Wing governing District Z, and showed them an item imbued with the power of The Wastes: a singularity. AE 185 Singularities Singularities are a concept of tremendous power, those corporations that sought to be wings and maintain their status needs to have a singularity to differentiate themselves from the rest as harnessing a singularity will bring in massive amounts of profits and military power. Singularities are well kept secrets, from objects that cry tears of rejuvination to be used as serums to heal farm animals from being slaughtered, to the preservation of bodies through a 20,000 year voyage into another dimension. Fixers were the errand boys of large corporations or people in wealth and/or in power, pay a fixer office or association to get a job done without having the guilt or shame of commiting it. Some fixers specialized in locating singularities specifically, being delvers of the ruins. With the singularities came imitations, or technology closely resembling their power or technology that could even rival their power, these technologies were often stolen for the benefit of the wings. A name for mercenaries became prevalent, often being called to fix a situation. AE 456 Patents The Head put a restriction of use of technologies, essentially a trademark for intellectual property. Now you could only use technologies of a different corporation if you had a license, like buying a commercial versions of their technology. Now the corporations that made them had an actual edge if they had an invention patented which bred competetiveness between each corporation and each wing, but each patent required that corporation to become unable to refuse service to The Head if they required their inventions. This didn't extend to singularities themselves, but it kept a leash on each wing and made The Head stronger as each corporation invented more technology. AE 788 Construct Uprising A corporation had constructed their own artificial intelligence that could learn by siphoning knowledge from the world wide web and repositories of projects of dead corporations about their technologies. The corporation allowed it to reitterate and construct the next model of artifical intelligence, eventually making itself capable of accessing databanks of wings and becoming knowlegable enough to grant itself the same technology without a patent. The corporation was later aprehended by The Head but the AI had already constructed an army using a string of orders to workshops through emails and made its entire nest a factory of unknowing artisans and created a force that could rival The Head by using tech of dead and new corporations. A war broke out against the artificial creations, only when each wing pooled their resources into snuffing the problem out did it finally subside, but the war against artificial intelligence and its constructs had led to each layer of the city to become uneven and some to sink or be seperated from its layer. It was then the taboos came into effect. AE 811 Taboos Taboos are laws of The Head that are universally enforced by The Claw and Arbiters of the city. The Claw and Arbiters are the primary force of The Head, each Arbiter and Claw consists of enough power to level an entire nest in one blow or able to teleport an entire building into The Wastes. When a taboo is broken, The Claw or an Arbiter is sent to deal with the problem, such as the creation or programming of an artificial being with autonomy comparable to that of humans. Some taboos have different punishments that are carried out as soon as possible; creating an artificial being with such autonomy results in the destruction of the entire corporation. If it was a wing, the entire nest if need be. Each nest began to adapt and even enforce their own taboos, creating taboo hunters that worked similar to The Claw but made up of hand picked individuals and were trained for the sole purpose of enforcing the law. These individuals were made to have their entire world revolve around the nest from the day they were born. AE 819 Syndicates and The Backstreets At some point, large gangs began to form. In the early days of the city, these gangs popped up like infestations, but were quickly dispatched by the Nests they were located in. In recent years, wars left scars across the Districts, and the Backstreetsâ€”the slums within those Districtsâ€”provided the gangs shelter to grow and become rival forces against Nest militaries and Fixers. The Syndicates began to lock down control of Backstreets and pressure Wings for ownership of Districts, preventing corporations from taking over without making a deal or forcing the syndicates away with power. Such disputes often turned into brawls as other syndicates joined in, hoping to be the ones who made the deal. These syndicates operated no differently from corporations, but their income wasn't from mass manufacturing; it came from selling illegal goods in Nests and Backstreets, robberies, and shaking down corporations and new or faltering Wings with their superior power. AE 1050 The Smoke War The Smoke War was a war between mortals and those that didn't look the part. G Corp. was a wing that created prosthetics for people, insect prosthetics. They were aligned with a power generating wing, L Corp., who created power via a singularity but generated insane amounts of smoke. At first, the smoke flew up into the sky, but after regulations were smacked on L Corp. after officials of the upper layer became bothered with the smoke, the smoke became heavy, and instead piled up like snow in the layers below it. The smoke war was incited by a rival corporation that made power through the creation of drugs that didn't have any side effects to the environment, so a war between wings naturally occured. The long standing L Corp. members did not wish for their cushy high life to go up in flames by a startup company, therefore they sought G Corp. and war did come. Many rallied behind the new L Corp. and supported the corporation, the smoke war was traumatising event where many lost sleep from the scenes of insects and the truth of the smoke that the war veterans of the smoke war were given amnesthics after many reports of sleepless nights and horrors that would haunt them into ending their own lives. AE 1052 White Night and Dark Days The New L Corp. fell in less than a year, less than 2 months. Their branches all over the city and the main branch itself came under fire from within, a pillar of light pierced the layers and the sky, lighting up the city in 3 days from the middle of L Corp. But suddenly, one day, the beam of light vanished and 4 dark days blanketed the entire city. The event was called The White Nights and Dark Days. After that event, creatures called abnormalities began to spring up from the rubble of L Corp. branches and began wreaking havoc in the city before being dispatched, captured by wings, or disappearing. Then, a few months after the event of The White Nights and Dark Days, people began to distort into strange humanoid creatures that were close to abstract concepts but eventually became known as abnormalities, at the same time, some people began to create and summon equipment out of nowhere. Records from L Corp. soon uncovered that they were researching equipment known as E.G.O, but the reason for why people are being turned into abnormalities or people being able to manifest E.G.O equipment out of thin air remains a mystery, or a gated secret. The Old World Documents that precede The Empire's records talk about a world without magic, a world of seven continents that's connected by an ocean. For clarity, we'll refer to this world as The Old World going forward. The Old World was said to be detached from other realms, including the elemental planes or the influence of gods and outer gods. They worshipped idols and gods through practice of scriptures and saw good fortune as signs of their god's attention. They were also an advanced race comparable to the era of the later patent wars. Rumors amongst elvenkind talk about The Old World being flooded after first contact of a deity, though dwarves and some secluded goblin settlements tell tales of The Old World persisting as the forgotten foundation of our own world. The thought of The Old World being underneath our planet brings many radical ideas, but connects the dots of some documents we recovered from The Empire about The Empyrean War. The Empyrean War The Empyrean War has been a matter of debate for a few centuries after the remains of The Empire was found and records of the war have been openly confiscated and restricted both by The Followers of The Pantheon and The Head. What is known about the war is that it was a war of the gods, their apostles, and their followers, of which there was no victor. Many agree it to be cause of why the world outside of Elysium is currently inhospitable for most creatures, but only a few dare to speculate about the cause of the war as it is a sensitive topic that could be seen as an offense to The Followers of The Pantheon. The Empire Records of The Empire state as a fact that it is a civilisation where it was directly influenced by a deity and where they gifted the bloodline of the throne the blood of the gods. The Empire is seen as the victor of The Empyrean War, not because it was confirmed with evidence, but because of the lack of records of any other settlement or kingdom that existed in its era. Almost all long lived races have no memory of The Empire or the world before the construction of Elysium, as if an act of divine intervention prevented its recollection, so we cannot confirm if the populace of Elysium are direct descendants of the people of The Empire. The Mana Fallout After retrieving records and books from The Empire, later books, or well, the last books that the imperials wrote was about a fallout of wild magic, where forests errode or decay in seconds, rivers of water become portals to other planes, and a rolling dense suffocating fog of mana blanketed the entire planet. Many speculate that it was the early stages of the apocalypse The Empire named The Mana Fallout. Treatment records describe races aligned with magic or directly inheriting bloodlines of magical beings such as true dragons or elementals started to age quicker- no, decay. Those that spent their life around magic would see similar effects, elves, genasi, druids, wizards, and many more began to age as if they were goblins. Many of the elderly died of quick, some races were pushed close to extinction and were forced to built bunkers. Bunkers we first thought as vaults or neighbouring ruins of Elysium. Formation of The Lunar Wastes Had all went well with the plans of The Imperials to bunker down, the world would have recovered after a few centuries and persevered, if not for the ocean becoming a planar doorway for celestial bodies to pass through and suddenly merge into the planet from the inside out. The deities prophesized of the event and attempted to preserve what little of the realm they could as well as their follower. The sudden inner collision of the ocean of the world birthing one of the planet's moons would be the end of our world if not for the direct intervention of the gods. The aftermath of the collision left the remains of the realm in a flux, creating the surface of the planet we now call The Lunar Wastes. 1 AE Discovery of The Ruins At some point, our ancestors had begun to leave their bunkers to search for a new home, many died in the pilgrimage but the gods directed their faithful to a land of promise. The Ruins of Elysium stood above The Wastes and the waves of erosion. They were directed to build a city, the last bastion of mortals to continue living within the realm. 14 AE The City of Elysium When The City of Elysium was raised, the gods of minor portfolios began to direct their followers to other realms to seek refuge, though a collection of greater gods made a Pantheon as an agreement to aid the development of Elysium collectively. Technology and magic were quickly improved, but the power of their followers amongst the survivors of The Lunar Wastes began to rise sharply... 114 AE Patent War The Patent War was a conflict of property, the scriptures, technology, and traditions of an entire community or religion copied by idol worshipers and those that worship outer influences that was not of the divine. They stole chants, hymns, magic, and identities and aligned themselves against the followers of the gods. It started a never ending arms race between The Pantheon's followers and the rest of the populace who wanted to covet the power of faith of The Pantheon but live outside of its order. 667 AE Construct Uprising When technology was reached, the unfaithful worshippers of non-divinity began to construct bodies of free labor to fight against the evergrowing faith of the people of The Pantheon. The first non-mortal was made in Elysium, it wasn't the first in history as there had been many records of automated humanoid machinery in the history of The Empire, but these machines were built to advise, act, and learn from The Pantheon's people. They began to mirror emotion, powers, and faith directed to gods outside of The Pantheon, this led to the liberation of artificial intelligence from the confines of their programming, aided by outer gods to take over Elysium. This conflict did the impossible, uniting the unfaithful and faithful factions of Elysium. 704 AE The Taboos After the Construct Uprising started, The Pantheon's followers and a new government body called The Head, worked together to surpress constructs of all kinds. Destroying aritifiial intelligence and purging it from all devices, dumping every line of code into the waves of The Lunar Wastes to erode into non-existence. Afterwards, regulations against the creation of constructs later formed, a specific set of regulations called "The Taboos" were set into motion. Taboos were actions that were forbidden from being commited within the city, the act of doing any of the taboos would lead to immediate execution, namely the creation of mechanical non-decomposing bodies that had autonomy and the use of technology or magic patented by companies, religious groups, workshops, etc. that reside in the city. 744 AE The Smoke War The Smoke War was a war between mortals and those that didn't want to be. The war started from a new corporation being a massive energy provider for large Districts of the city. The pollution of its method to generate energy was fair, but it only grew worse and soon the District that the corporation resided in became inhospitable. The officials of the District, instead of putting backlash on the corporation, began to produce products to help cope with living within the District to profit off of the common folk's suffering. Everything went well until the pollution got to the point of overflowing onto other Districts of the city till breathable air became a commodity. War broke out and what spilled onto the battlefield weren't humanoids, but humanoids shaped into insectoids as if they were clay put into a mold of insects. These were the products they were being sold by the District to help cope with the smoke, not inhalers or masks, but body part replacements. Despite their grotesque appearance, Elysium recognized these replacements as products of the District and official prosthesis. title: The Middle - Lore - Fable
text: General : The Middle The City General Elysium Timeline Districts The Middle is one of the Five Fingers of the Backstreets, operating with a focus on supporting one another and punishing anyone who disrespects them. Like the other Fingers, the Middle is one of the most powerful Syndicates in the City, possessing enough influence to rival even the Wings. Overview Like the other four Fingers, the Middle is a large Syndicate with a unique culture and creed that all members follow fervently. Members operate on an extremely tight-knit 'familial' structure, enjoying close fraternal ties with one another. Reflective of their bonds, everyone in the Middle refers to each other as their "Brothers", "Sisters", or "Siblings". While the Middle cherishes its own members, it takes the polar opposite approach towards outsiders. Any "sin" committed against a member of the Middle, their loved ones, or property is recorded in the "Book of Vengeance" so that the perpetrator might be punished for the deed. The Middle is well-known for never letting go of unfulfilled grudges, and members may spend years chasing down its enemies to enact justice, which often entails a punishment that is grossly disproportionate to the perceived crime. Besides listing the names of everyone who has slighted the Middle, the Book of Vengeance also provides guidelines for the punishment to every conceivable crime, which range from murdering a Sibling to the simple act of stepping on a member's shoe. The same list is shared across every Book of Vengeance, although said lists appear to be divided by District. Particularly high-risk Vengeances are classified as Labors and Big Siblings are expected to complete one in order to earn the title of Great Sibling. Depending on the crime, the Middle will not hesitate to annihilate everyone in the perpetrator's faction, town, or social circle.The Middle may not even care who actually committed the sin, and will just opt to enact mass vengeance against whoever in the vicinity in order to teach everyone nearby a lesson. On the other hand, members of the Middle are far more lenient to each other, and slights are generally ignored and forgiven out of loyalty to one another. However, members of the Middle are expected to be in the Syndicate for life, and thus nobody can leave it. Anyone who attempts to move on from the Syndicate will be hunted down by their former Siblings until they die or erase absolutely every indicator of the Middle from themselves. There exists no strict dress code among the Middle beyond blending in with other members. They tend to wear light-colored dress pants and garish shirts or coats in purple and pink tones, as well as carry around personal copies of the Book of Vengeance with them. Other common attributes include golden chains wrapped around the forearm, shins, and neck (larger amounts of chains are present on higher-ranking members), which the Middle utilize in combat, and are meant to symbolize solidarity and connection between Siblings. Members of the Middle are also recognizable by their enhancement tattoos; as they are allowed to get a single tattoo with each vengeance completed, the number of tattoos present on one's body tends to denote their ranking in the Syndicate. In combat, the Middle make use of punches and kicks, augmented by the tattoos, although they will occasionally make use of weapons as well, especially when conducting punishments. Hierarchy The Middle's hierarchy system features at least four major ranks, which do not appear to contain sub-ranks. The ranks are as follows: Little Sibling Young Sibling Big Sibling Great Sibling: The highest rank mentioned thus far. One of the requirements for promotion from Big Sibling to Great Sibling is completing a Pilgrimage of Loyalty, which involves accomplishing one or more Labors. While there are multiple ranks within the Syndicate, they do not seem to call for any difference in how members treat each other, as in-group relationships are built on mutual respect, care, and trust that succeeds any power structure. Instead, there exists a natural tendency for lower-ranking members to want to impress their superiors, and higher-ranking members to dote on their subordinates.

title: Offices - Lore - Fable
text: General : Offices The City General Elysium Timeline Districts Offices, rarely referred to as Fixer Offices, are businesses founded and operated by Fixers that take on various sorts of requests from clients for a price. Most Offices have a focus on combat of some kind, but there are a large variety of specializations an Office can have that range from protecting clients to gathering information to creating weapons and tools for other Fixers to use. The Associations, in particular the Hana Association which oversees all Fixer related activity in the City, manage and regulate Offices. Overview Offices are organized groups of Fixers that congregate to handle work together. Joining an Office is a necessity for virtually all Fixers, as it is the best way for them to receive contracts. Offices are lead by a Representative, typically shortened to Office Rep, that owns the business and manages the contracts accepted by the Office and oversees the other Fixers employed there. Office sizes can greatly vary, as Offices with around a dozen members are noted to be of small size, but it appears common for them to be formed by as little as three members. Fixers who prefer to work on their own can create and manage their own independent Office. The majority of Offices have a dress code that all members follow in order to give a desired impression to potential clients. Offices are managed by the twelve Associations according to their specializations and areas of expertise, with the Hana Association overseeing the various facets of their work and grading the Office accordingly. Similarly to the Fixer grading system, an Office can be promoted to a higher grade or be demoted. To operate, an Office must be recognized by the Hana Association, after which it can begin taking up contracts. Fledgling Offices start out taking on Open Contracts, contracts that are posted by the various Associations for Fixer Offices to pick up, operating on a first-come, first-serve basis, which allows the Office to start making a name for itself. As an Office gains notoriety in the industry, it becomes capable of picking up and receiving private contracts based on its Fixers' skills. Offices and the Fixers working for them may advertise and promote themselves in a variety of ways, including being featured in frequently updated magazines or catalogues, such as 'Fixers Monthly'. When an Office accepts a job, a contract is typically created between the client and the Office before the case can be dealt with. These contracts ensure that the client will pay for the services provided to them and that the Office will do their best to complete the job, and breaking a signed contract will not be overlooked by the Associations. If a contract is not made, or never signed by one of the parties, then neither the client nor Office is required to make good on their end of the deal. For contracts made between two Offices, it is typical for the Offices involved to use a notary public Office to officially certify the deal and prevent future issues. Many Offices attempt to have some level of uniqueness and marketability to make them stand out to potential clients, such as being made up of former Syndicate members or other, similar gimmicks. Some offer "pay for one request, get one for free" contract events to entice clients, but behind the scenes there are many technical aspects to such deals that benefit the Office more than the client, such as limiting the grade of the free contract or other aspects of the job. Other Offices operate differently from most others not out of a desire to draw in clients, but out of a moral code. For example, some Offices go as far as to ban their members from killing people, and refuse contracts that would require the taking of life. Others are managed differently from the typical Office, such as hereditary Offices, where ownership of the Office is passed down through a family, and its members highly value loyalty. One strict rule which is managed by both the Hana Association and the Öufi Association is that Fixers and Offices never threaten people into requesting them. After completing a request, a report to the Hana Association must be made that includes the details of the request, the client's information, how the request was solved, and any other relevant information. These reports are used by the Hana Association in their evaluations of Offices and Fixers and inform the grades assigned to them. Most Offices are direct affiliates of one of the Associations. Affiliated Offices typically specialize in a related field to the Association they work under, such as the Offices that monitor the deals and gambling of J Corp.'s casinos often being affiliated with the Öufi Association. Not being affiliated with an Association is seen as untrustworthy, and carries the risk of clients fearing that Office could be associated with a Syndicate. Some Offices are more than just affiliated, and are instead Associate Offices which essentially work directly on the Association's orders. Being an Associate Office comes with significant advantages, as the Association assigns jobs to the Offices rather than them having to find jobs on their own, and they get paid a stable salary. Thanks to the job security, it is easier for the Fixers of the Office to have a peaceful day to day life as they don't need to deal with clients directly like a non-affiliated Office does. That said, Associate Offices do not have the ability to turn down jobs from their affiliated Association, even when the contract puts the Office at risk of being wiped out. Offices will often form partnerships with multiple other Offices to help cover for areas outside of their specialty and to assist when an accepted job is more complicated than it first appeared. Partnered Offices can be called in for reinforcements or professional aid in specific areas. Beyond just partnered Offices, some Offices are sister Offices and share more information with each other than they would a partnered Office. These sister Offices are normally formed by close friends, or people who had worked closely together in the past, who are now Representatives of their own respective Office, and will go to greater lengths to help each other than they would for other Offices. Workshops Workshops are a type of Fixer Office that specialize in the production of weapons, gear, and other tools used by Fixers, including customized orders. Workshops typically aim to create products to match the needs of the typical Fixer, but some highly regarded Workshops that can afford to be more selective with their clientele work on a membership system, with the owners of the Workshop picking and choosing their clients. As Workshops are still officially classified as Fixer Offices, they can accept more typical Fixer contracts that are unrelated to their inventions and sales. Known Offices Office Name Explanation Rosespanner Workshop Rosespanner Workshop is a Workshop active in the K Corp. Backstreets. While it is a small Workshop, its Fixers carry out a variety of tasks, with some of them mostly handling "indoor work" such as communication with clients, and others handling "outdoor work", meaning more typical combat requests. MultiCrack Office The MultiCrack Office is an Office made up exclusively of Fixers with Prosthetics.The Multicrack Office is an Office that only accepts applications from Fixers with prosthetics, as prosthetic users are able to better withstand fatigue and fear during battle. Multicrack Office Fixers typically have multiple arms prosthetic arms, which allows the Fixers to switch to the models best suited to the mission they're to be deployed in, and which, when broken, can be quickly exchanged with replacement arms mid-battle. Beside those, they have a variety of augmentations, ranging from limb prosthetics, to eyesight and hearing augmentations, including full-body prosthetics as well. Fanghunt Office -The Fanghunt Office is an Office of Fixers specialized in hunting Bloodfiends and Vampires. Fixers of Fanghunt Office uniformly wear black or dark grey clothing with numerous rhomboid silver decorations and accessories, and fight with large mallets with spikes, resembling meat tenderizers. A cartridge belt slung across the shoulder contains vials of water and potentially styptics (drugs that inhibit bleeding). Dawn Office Dawn Office may be small, but that doesn't take away from its Fixers' competence. Each of its Fixers is skilled enough to handle Urban Legend-grade requests on their own, which is no easy feat. Furthermore, its Fixers cooperate well with each other and have a harmonious, almost familial relationship. Dawn Office's specialty is direct combat, with workshop weapons that generate heat. Wedge Office Wedge Office is an Office which specializes in precise situational analysis to excel in combat.Although Wedge Office is a combat-oriented Office, its specialty is not in direct combat prowess. Instead, clients who hire Wedge Office come seeking its Fixers' analytical skills, studying opponents' weaknesses to strike them down as precisely and efficiently as possible. However, this specialization leaves Wedge Office at a disadvantage against large groups of enemies. Hook Office The Hook Office is a murder-for-hire Office composed of former Syndicate members, known for its brutal conduct and capacity for messy jobs like contract killings and gruesome executions. Full-Stop Full-Stop Office is rare amongst Offices for using firearms. Such weapons are unpopular with most Fixers because of the severe restrictions the Head's laws place on them, the heavy taxes the Head places on ammunition, and the specialized training needed to actually handle a firearm.
